utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Good afternoon to you, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are present. From the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Meek and the return of Mr. Ostojic and Ms. Condon. The Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Vanderpuye. I understand there are some preliminaries. If they are not related to the rest of the evidence of this witness I suggest that we first finish with this witness and then raise the issues before the next one comes along. All right? So let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Dragutinovic. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hopefully we'll finish within a short time, so I just remind you that you are still testifying under oath. Mr. Vanderpuye, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dragutinovic. Yesterday, in relation to some questions I put to you regarding the involvement of the security organ in the schools, you had indicated that you had reviewed the duty operations notebook. I wanted to show you an entry from that notebook. Could I have 65 ter 377, please, in e-court? And could we page forward to ERN 02935796, please? Thank you. Is it possible to have the translation also placed upon the screen or no? I'll just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The date is the 23rd of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Do you have the page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Of where the date is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The page number of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, it's not among the previously translated pages but I can have the witness read it to the extent that he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, I'd just like to direct your attention if I could, to the entry that begins with 031854389. And I wonder if you could read that entry into the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Skelani have two" -- it could be injured, the next word could be injured, "Turks - I said to kill them off because Bratunac does not want to receive them." I think that's what it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This was an entry that was made by the duty operations officer the 23rd of July 1995. Have you seen this entry before, Mr. Dragutinovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. And I know who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that direction consistent with your view that the prisoners were treated fairly and consistently with the Geneva Convention, as you testified previously?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is written here is by no means in keeping with the Geneva Conventions or what I said before, but it does not necessarily reflect the general situation at the Zvornik Brigade because the person who wrote this appeared here as a witness. I believe he made a statement concerning this. And I would not like to comment upon it. He has been interrogated, questioned, and he had to explain the reason why he wrote this. As for these people, Skelani have nothing to do with the Zvornik Brigade and the person who called the Zvornik Brigade, frankly, I don't know why they called, this battalion does not belong to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that I don't see any connection, so as I said, the person who wrote this appeared before you as a witness and you must have asked him to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When did you learn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is he referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was just going to ask him that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The duty operations officer, I believe it was Mr. Ljubo Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Ljubo Bojanovic was your subordinate during that period of time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, he was already part of the section for morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when did you learn that he made this entry into the duty officer's notebook?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't review everything, so I learned about this later, somewhat later, and we were unable to check and find out what happened to the people concerned in this entry. Ljubo Bojanovic's comment or explanation was that we had nothing to do with it, and it was -- well, I can hardly call it a slip, but as I said before, you must have asked him for an explanation and he must have given you one. I wouldn't like to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well. You don't have any personal information as to what happened to the prisoners that are mentioned in this particular entry, do you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a different area altogether. You had mentioned that following your return from the vicinity of Zepa around the 15th of July forward, that there were units from the 16th -- it was a unit from the 16th Krajina Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May we have a reference so that we can keep up with exactly what the -- my colleague is referring to so we know when this question was asked and what context so we may assess whether it is properly within the scope of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Do you have the specific reference you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do. It's at transcript page 12, line 7 -- well, page 12706 to page 12707.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: These were questions that were put to you by my colleague, Mr. Haynes. In particular, you can start on page 12706, line 10 and we can go through line 19, if you would like, if it would satisfy my colleague, I could read the exact question and answer into the record but I'll ask the witness if he recalls. I think that will probably be quicker. Do you recall having mentioned in your testimony that there was a unit from the Krajina in or around the area where you were between the 16th to the 18th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That unit was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That unit, was it under the control of your commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit was resubordinated to the command of the Zvornik Brigade as soon as they came to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as best as you recall, when was it that they came to the Zvornik Brigade or were subordinated to the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigade was brought into the area of the 7th Battalion in the evening of the 6th -- sorry, not brigade, company. And I was with that company on the 17th and the 18th, and it could have arrived like two days prior.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Can I just have P02838 in e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, in the area where you were, were you in communication with this unit from the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening of the 17th -- 16th, on the 17th and on the 18th. Only during the day of the 18th, not in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware, was that unit in contact with the forward command post where your commander was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I know. The only possibility is that the company commander was taken to the forward command post or maybe somebody from the command led that company to a different location in the field and later on the company was resubordinated to us on the 15th or something like that, but the whole company did not go to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information regarding the participation of that unit in the execution of Muslim prisoners during the period of time that they were resubordinated to your brigade? And in particular, on or about the 19th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. All right, Mr. Dragutinovic. Thank you for your time. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Dragutinovic, as you see, we have managed to conclude your testimony within a relatively short time today, which enables you to go back home at the earliest. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for being kind enough to come over and give testimony, and on behalf of everyone I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We come to the document exhibit tendering process now. The Prosecution, you've got four documents to tender; is that correct? Basically they are --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have the duty officer's notebook, 377, Mr. President, that I would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I want to make sure that I do not have any confusion here. I'm asking you to combine together documents that you use and wish to tender, both in the course of your examination-in-chief and your redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. We have two documents that we wish to tender from the direct, which are 65 ter 318 and 65 ter 689. We have from the redirect, we have 65 ter 377, 65 ter 1309 and 1310. Those are the intercepts which have already been marked for identification and will stay that way. 65 ter 962 which was the 15th July interim combat report. 65 ter 341, which was the 23rd July combat report, daily combat report. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Before I ask the Defence teams for their remarks, I'm informed that 65 ter number 377, which Mr. Vanderpuye used during his redirect has already been used and introduced with Witness Jovicic, and that was marked for identification purposes. That's just for your information. Now, any objections to the admittance of any of these documents, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No objection. I wonder whether we could just have an update on the translation of P377, because it's becoming a bit of a nuisance, not being able to use it fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know who can enlighten us, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have made inquiries. We are still trying to determine from CLSS which portions have been translated at the defence's request so we can integrate them with ours and I'm awaiting an assessment from our team translation people to find out how much in total is left. So we are still determining that. I can't give you a time estimate on how long it's going to take to translate the remainder but we are actually optimistic. I spoke with our team person yesterday. She believes at least the second half of the entire notebook has been translated which just leaves whatever is left from the first half, that the Defence has not already requested to be translated. That's my understanding at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Any objections from anyone? None? So 377, there is no need for it to be tendered again because it has been marked for identification already. 1309 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are trying to find out here whether the reason for marking for identification, document 65 ter number 377 was only the absence of translation or whether there was any other reason or objection behind which or on the basis of which -- yes, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My recollection, Mr. President, is that that was the only hangup with respect to that document, as both sides have liberally used, and I believe intend to continue to liberally use the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So seems to be also the impression of Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. President I just wanted to point out that based on the witness's testimony today with respect to Ljubo Bojanovic in particular, we will be seeking to introduce his prior testimony pursuant to 92 quater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The pleasure is yet to come, sort of. So we are talking of 65 ter number 1309 A, B and C; 1310 A, B and C; 962; and 341. These are 65 ter numbers. And then again, 318 and 689. All right. I think out of deference, I would go to the Pandurevic Defence team documents. You have distributed a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not proposing to go through it. Can I acknowledge one failing with the list? I had intended that there should be some analysis in the document of which of these exhibits have already been tendered into evidence because I'm sure that some of them have, and I'm sure that can be attended to before the end of today's sitting and that will simplify this process. It's explicit as to the absence of translation of documents and I think in the next column along, MFI can be written next to any document which has no English translation but if you would give me just the opportunity of checking which of the 42 documents have already been tendered into evidence, we can finalise this process much more simply at a later stage in the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think Madam Registrar will also look into that because it will show up on her computer and simplify it. They have a programme for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Aren't they lucky?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime I would like to know whether there is any objection from the Prosecution side to any of these documents after which I will ask the other Defence teams whether they object to the admission of any of these documents. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have none, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any of the other Defence teams wishes to object? None. So subject to verification, all these documents are being admitted. Those which are -- that have not yet been translated will obviously be marked for identification purposes pending translation thereof. And those which have already been tendered through previous witnesses will not be considered tendered again. Those are the only two caveats, all right? Thank you, Mr. Haynes. And thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. I think Miletic Defence team, you have also circulated a document listing the documents you wish to tender, mostly they are entries in the regular -- from the regular combat report which you referred to earlier on in one of your submissions, Madam Fauveau. And it also shows which ones have been translated and which ones haven't. Actually almost none of them have been translated. Maybe one or two. Any objection on your part, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't ask you but I thought I had covered -- do you wish to state anything, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection from any of the Defence teams? None. So these documents are admitted with the usual caveat, those that have not yet received a translation will in the meantime and until they are so translated remain marked for identification. Thank you. Nikolic Defence team, you've got two documents that you wish to tender 3D165 and 3D166, which is also 37 -- which is 65 ter number 379. Are there -- yes, Madam Nikolic? Are there any objections on your part, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There are none, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the other Defence teams? We hear none. So the first one of these will remain marked for identification. You have a draft translation, but we require a proper, formal one, unless you are happy with the draft translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are happy with the draft translation, but just to be sure, we will be providing an official translation as is the usual practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's take the usual course. We'll mark it for identification pending official translation thereof. The second one, second document, is admitted. There are no other Defence teams that wish to tender any documents with this witness, Dragutinovic? None. So that closes that chapter. And we now come to the preliminary matter that you wish to raise, Mr. Zivanovic. One moment, because I think Madam Registrar wants to raise something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1309 and 1310, I don't think there is a need to have them readmitted because they have already been admitted previously. And marked for identification actually. So Mr. Zivanovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to address the Trial Chamber regarding the Prosecution witness 128, but considering the sensitive and confidential nature of this information, I would like to go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, of course, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't understand how that can be irrelevant, namely the fact that the Prosecutor clearly violated the rules of evidence and procedure, consistently with Article 43, when the Prosecutor questions a suspect that has to be recorded. The fact that there was a change of status during the interview does not change this fact in any way. So if the Prosecutor didn't have the necessary equipment with him, he could interrupt the interview and bring the equipment the next day. I find it inadmissible that we receive three pages of notes to cover an interview that was four hours long and during two and a half out of those four hours the witness was in the status of a suspect, and the claim of the Prosecutor that this is irrelevant, I find inadmissible and unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Apart from the relevance or irrelevance thing, the thing is it seems that what's -- there's no remedy to this. They don't exist. There is no video recording and there are no further notes than what you have been given. So what do you want? I mean us to declare that the whole interview was at least as to 50 per cent irregularly conducted and therefore you should even -- the Prosecution should not have even given you the report, interview report or whatever it's called? I think we better stick to what is really pertinent now, the issue of whether we should delay the testimony of this gentleman or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau. You may sit down, I'll ask you to intervene soon, very soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I'm concerned, this witness doesn't concern my client at all. However, I am personally very concerned with a procedure that the Prosecutor followed. For my part, I want a clear explanation from the Prosecutor how it was possible to question a witness, a suspect in fact, for two and a half hours without any recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I would have allowed as much time as possible to discuss this, if the person you were representing was that witness. I mean we are talking of something completely different here. I mean, if there was an irregularity, the complainant, strictly speaking, should be that person and as far as you are concerned, you almost consider yourself lucky that at least you have a document that has been made available. Yes, Mr. Ostojic and then Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, on two points, Mr. President if I may. What's curious is that my learned friend from the Prosecution says that the notes are not available or he says is not available. If you look at-- if we look at it, the information report and the interview was conducted on the 29th of October 2002, the information report was not generated immediately thereafter but two weeks later on the 11th of November 2002. For him to simply suggest to you that there are no notes available really calls into question how is it that, within two weeks, they were able to create this information report, having no notes, not even telling us whether they ever had notes, whether they were ultimately destroyed and why. Secondly, I agree with Your Honour that there is no remedy. The prejudice does exist but there is no remedy. The remedy offered by the Prosecution that we can call back this witness is woefully inadequate and they should not only follow the rules but we see in other instances when this individual, 128, was considered a witness, they tape-recorded him. Those tapes don't exist. We do see that there is a transcript showing tape 1, side A and B, et cetera. When he's converted into a suspect four years ago, four and a half years ago, they don't follow up with another interview with him or conduct an interview categorising him as a suspect as they qualified him as being. It's a violation of the rules. I agree with the Court there is no remedy, however my client has been prejudiced as a result of this. Nothing in his prior interviews that have been conducted does he reference or mention Mr. Beara at all in those interviews. Surprisingly, in some summary fashion through third or fourth party sources, there is a reference of approximately one or two lines to my client which comes new but there is no record of it that this witness said it. We have not interviewed this witness, we have not discussed with this witness at any time, although counsel said that some have. I just want the record to be clear on that. They had the notes because they couldn't have conducted the information report two weeks after the interview. They tell us that it's not available but we would like an explanation because it's a direct violation of the rules, and quite candidly, there is no remedy but there is prejudice to my client and I believe to the rest of the Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rules mention video recording, not necessarily the taking down of notes but I think, let's conclude on this. Do you know of the existence of these notes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very quickly, Your Honour. The investigator present was contacted yesterday, he's no longer with the Tribunal, and said that those notes were destroyed after he -- after the information report was done. So I didn't say there were no notes taken during the interview but those notes were later destroyed at some point before he left the Tribunal, after he had written the information report. The tape recordings of the two tape-recorded interviews are available, the ones from 2001 and 2002. So I don't know what my friend was referring to there. This is the first we've ever had -- request we've had is in this courtroom today for those tape recordings of those transcripts. Those are available, I'm sure, and I think I've answered his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it to be yesterday, at least. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With all due respect, Mr. President, I have some difficulty understanding the Trial Chamber saying to us that we are lucky to have some information coming from a witness when it is the duty of the Prosecution when they meet a witness to provide us with what the witness has said. That's normal disclosure. I don't think we are lucky to have this information. I think it is owed to us. But that's not the most important point, Mr. President. It's that there is during such a -- the interview that took place which gave rise to the production of the information report, during the segment of the interview it is mentioned that the status of the witness was changed to that of a suspect and that's what it said, he was not being truthful about the identification of the soldiers being present at Rocevic school. For this reason, they changed the status of the witness to that of a suspect. Once a suspect, during an interview that lasts two and a half hours, the witness provided new information, not previously mentioned in any of his interviews, as well as information which contradicts information in his two previous interviews, now, as a Defence counsel, I want to represent my client and knowing how is it that this witness changed his mind during the interview and how is it that this witness could have provided new information because he was under pressure of being a suspect. At the end of the interview, once the Prosecution is satisfied about what information has been received, then they change the status back to that of a normal witness. So for two and a half hours, this is the information, Mr. President, that we would like to have. Now, contrary to what my colleague has said, I believe that there is an existing remedy. The remedy is twofold. First of all, as a minimum, we would ask to have, to know whether my colleague, Mr. McCloskey, senior trial attorney, present at the Tribunal for many years, whether he took any notes during that interview and whether he has any notes because he was conducting that interview. Secondly, we would like to have from the Office of the Prosecution a reassurance whether it be by the chief of Prosecution or the chief of investigation that when investigators leave the Tribunal, they do leave their stuff behind and that notes are not destroyed. This is the property of the Tribunal. It's the only record we have of what really happened during that interview because they failed to abide by the rules, and also, if there is new information mentioned in the information report, I believe that the remedy simply should be that the Prosecution should not be authorised to lead any questions to the witness concerning this new information. Mr. President, that addresses only the part about this -- the fact that the interview wasn't recorded. But I also would like to address the Chamber concerning the other issue and I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So following your submissions, we need to have some time to -- for consultations. We will have the break now instead of 15 minutes' time and it will be a 30-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we realised when we were discussing that Mr. Bourgon did refer to you, in the sense that we don't know, we haven't been told, whether you, who were present there during the interview, kept any notes yourself. And then the other issue, namely whether it is the practice in the OTP that when investigators leave the Tribunal, they leave their stuff behind rather than destroy notes. Do you have anything to or do you wish to state anything in regard to these two submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can respond to the Court's inquiry. Yes, I was at that interview. I've been at a lot of interviews over ten years. I generally do not -- I have an outline but I didn't keep notes. That's why there is always an investigator there, and the issue of investigators, whether or not they destroy their notes, that is normally, has been in the past, left up to the investigator. Many police departments have that policy that when you type up your report you destroy the notes. I don't know about this particular situation, though. I know that we -- I believe, well, Mr. Bursik's been contacted by another investigator but I have not, nor has Mr. Nicholls spoken to him. If there is any more details that are needed but that's the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have discussed and come to a conclusion. We will communicate our conclusion to you either at the end of this session or after the next break. We just need to formulate the few bullet points which are at the basis of it. So now, next witness? And this is -- he hasn't got any protective measures, does he? We are talking of --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a brief preliminary with respect to this witness before he's brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does he need a caution?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: He does, and I had a discussion with him about protective measures. He may feel more at ease if he hears a brief explanation or description from Your Honour about the parameters that the Trial Chamber follows concerning granting protective measures. I've explained it to him. He understands; I think it might make him feel a little more comfortable just to hear it from the Trial Chamber. I'm not asking for protective measures. I've explained to him that given the circumstances he described, that they most likely would not be forthcoming given the prior practice of this Trial Chamber. He's comfortable with that. He has concerns based on the fact that he is a police officer. He is concerned about being contacted by journalists. He is concerned that he's being called by the Prosecution. I explained to him that his employer has indicated, which is the MUP, has basically required that he be here pursuant to our request. I've indicated to him that the fact that he's concerned about journalists or the fact that he's a police officer does not rise to the level, in the Prosecution's opinion, to warrant formally applying for the protective measures. He understands that. If the Court would indulge my request, I think it might make him feel more comfortable also hearing it from the Trial Chamber. I understand if the Trial Chamber does not desire to intervene in that process. I understand why the Chamber would not want to. I just offer that as a suggestion for the sake of the witness's comfort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have an understanding counsel, an understanding witness, and a request to the Trial Chamber. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does any one of the Defence teams wish to address this issue? I don't think so but anyway, okay. We'll come back to you very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way we will go about it is this: We have not been seized with a motion for protective measures so you understand that our intervention will be very limited. We will convert ourselves into private session for a short while, while he walks in, he sits down, I'll interview him a minute or two, and then we will proceed. So let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, we are going to proceed -- we are not yet -- we are going to proceed now in open session. The witness has made a solemn declaration to testify the truth. Mr. Thayer will go first. He will ask you some questions and then he will be followed by the various Defence teams on cross-examination. Before you start giving evidence, I need to remind you also of a special right that exists under our rules relating to witnesses. And it basically says the following. There are some witnesses who, if they are asked some questions which they are compelled to answer, could lead them to incrimination, possible incrimination. We have a hedge. We have a right in our rules to try and protect witnesses from being compelled to answer questions which could possibly incriminate them in the future. But it is not an absolute right. In such a case, if a question is put to you which you have an objection to, because it could tend to incriminate you, you first need to ask for our intervention and explain to us your contention. We might agree with you or we might decide to disagree with you. Obviously if we agree with you, you will be exempted from answering that question. If we disagree with you, we will compel you to answer those questions. But if you give answers, you make statements in answer to such questions because you are compelled by the Trial Chamber and not because you wanted to, then your statement would not be able, will not be used as evidence against you in any subsequent Prosecution that might be taken against you, except if you are prosecuted for false testimony, which at the moment is beside the point. So have I explained this right clear to you? All right. And were you aware of that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Were you aware of that before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Thayer, he's in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dobrisav Stanojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just how old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 36 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in a village Zalazje, that's in Srebrenica municipality and I was raised in Srebrenica. My documents list the village of Obadi as my place of birth but that's the local commune. I was in fact born in the village of Zalazje.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you identify yourself as a Bosnian Serb, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Trial Chamber how you're currently employed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now, I work at the dog training centre in Bratunac which is part of the Republika Srpska police administration. Up until that time, I worked in Srebrenica, and then at my request I was transferred to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when did you first begin working in Srebrenica prior to going to the dog training centre, and in what capacity were you employed when you were employed in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was transferred to Srebrenica on the 1st of January 1997, and I was just an ordinary police officer, and at that time, while I worked in Srebrenica, I was the sector leader, and then I became the shift leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just can you put a year on when you went to the canine training unit?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I'd like to do now, sir, is review with you briefly your military service history, and if I may I'd just like to summarise it to move things along a little bit more quickly if I could. And please correct me when I'm done if I've misstated anything or left anything out, okay? In the spring of 1992, you joined a unit called the Srebrenica Guard which consisted of about 30 soldiers who were refugees from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That unit, the Srebrenica Guard, was dismantled in mid-1992 and became part of the Bratunac Brigade, its 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were subsequently transferred from the army to the MUP, municipal police, in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you explain just briefly why you were transferred, if you know, to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not able to give you a specific answer. I was just an ordinary soldier. I think there was a request made by the police station for somebody from Srebrenica, a refugee from Srebrenica, should join the police in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you receive any training from the MUP for your new position? And if so, where was that training?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I underwent training. I completed a police training course in Jahorina. That was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were you assigned after completing that training, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the police station in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just generally speaking, what were your duties at the police station in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was a police officer, a beat police officer, and I just performed everyday police duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe, please, the command structure at that time of the police station in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the names or just the functions?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Both, if you would, just perhaps the top two levels in the structure.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the top two, the police station chief was Mr. Luka Bogdanovic, and the police station commander was Mr. Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at some point, was Mr. Borovcanin replaced as the commander of that station? And if so, do you recall approximately when?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubisa Borovcanin left to take up a new function in the Special Police unit. I think it was sometime in late 1993 or early 1994. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to turn to a slightly different topic for just a couple of questions. In addition to your regular police duties, did you also serve in a PJP company?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And which company was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 1st Company of the PJP that was part of the Zvornik centre. Of course, it was part of the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say the Zvornik centre, do you mean the Zvornik public security centre, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's the public security centre Zvornik, the Zvornik public security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Trial Chamber has already heard testimony about how PJP companies are made up of policemen from municipal police stations belonging to a particular centre. Can you recall for the Trial Chamber from which police stations the 1st Zvornik PJP company was formed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Company consisted of the Zvornik police station, the Milici police station, Vlasenica, Sekovici, Bratunac and Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 1st Company?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radomir Pantic, Raso Pantic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was the company subdivided into smaller units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was divided into three platoons, the 1st, the 2nd and the 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who was your platoon commander, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Police officer Dusan Micic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, just generally speaking, sir, what duties did you carry out as a PJP member?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing special. I was just a member of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when you were a member of the PJP, would you be deployed on occasion to the field?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Depending on the actual needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could just give the Trial Chamber just a general idea of what kind of tasks you performed as a PJP member in the field?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depending on the situation and our involvement, we would mostly be deployed when the Muslim units would perform raids in our territories, when the lines would be broken through, and then in cooperation with the army, we would put a stop to the Muslim army advances.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how often were you deployed in the field?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, depending on the actual needs. Sometimes a month would go without our going out and then we would go two or three times within the next month and then for three months we would go maybe once. It all depended on the actual situation. But there was no rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were not in the field, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular police duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And sir, when you were deployed as a PJP member would you ever see Special Police Brigade units operating in the same area as you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what kind of tasks did the Special Police Brigade units carry out?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. I'm not sure about their activities. I think that they were mostly engaged in combat and I don't know anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that's fine, sir. Would you characterise the nature of the tasks that you carried out as a PJP member as the same types of combat tasks that the Special Police Brigade typically carried out or were your tasks different in any way, generally speaking, from those of the Special Police Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in the field, they were almost the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when were you deployed in the field with your PJP unit, did you wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did the uniform consist in, sir? Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was green, a green camouflage pattern uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you wear any insignia or emblems or patches on your uniform, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My unit had the insignia indicating that it was the 1st Company of the Zvornik centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what type of equipment were you issued?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing in -- nothing special. We were issued weapons, bullet-proof vests, uniforms and also sets of ammunition for our weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you ever carry hand grenades, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to turn your attention to July of 1995. At that time, were you still serving as a regular policeman in the Bratunac police station and as a PJP member?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to focus on the time of the VRS attack on the Srebrenica enclave. During the first week of July, when the VRS attacked the enclave, did you or your PJP unit take part in that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During the second week of July 1995, did you receive an order to report somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 11th, in the afternoon, we received an order to report to the police station with all our combat equipment and to wait there for the rest of the unit to join us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall how you received that order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly. I think that one of my colleagues conveyed it to me. I don't know whether I was at home or in the street. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what if anything were you told about what the purpose of reporting to the police station was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was said. The only thing that was said is that we should wait for the rest of the unit to join us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to unit, sir, what exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Company of the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, where did you spend the evening of or the night of July 11th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon my arrival to the police station, we stayed there for a while, and then I and a couple of other colleagues went to a neighbourhood at the outskirts of the town because there was a farewell party or a wedding party, I don't know what it was. We stayed there for a while. The duty police officer knew where we were. And when I returned from the feast I remained in the police station. I slept a little bit and I stayed there until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the 1st Company, in fact, arrived that night?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that they had arrived, but I myself did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So the next day, on July 12th, just tell the Trial Chamber what you did, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning of the 12th, one of my colleagues drove me in an official vehicle to the Yellow Bridge. There, my unit was already there at the Yellow Bridge and I joined them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what information, if any, did you receive at that time about what was going on in that area of Yellow Bridge and Potocari, and if anything about the assignment that you were about to embark on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive any information. I was a bit late arriving there. Everybody else was already there when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I joined the rest of the unit and we waited to advance further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And at some point, did you in fact advance?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before moving on, there was an incident in which a soldier was killed by a mine. We waited for the soldier to be carried away. And then we deployed in a line, in a firing line, and moved towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple of quick follow-up questions, sir. First, the soldier who was killed, do you know what role or specialty that soldier had who was killed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a member of the Bratunac Brigade, and he was a mine expert or bomb disposal person. I think that's what he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you described that you were deployed in a firing line, and I'm just going to ask you to describe what you mean by that first, and what was your task as you were deployed? What were you told that you were to expect, if anything, as you were deployed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our objective -- well, at the time when I arrived, nothing was said to me, but when we started to deploy, I learned from my colleagues that we would have to search the terrain and to take the right-hand side of the hill, and to go all the way down to Potocari in order to search the terrain, looking for any remaining Muslim army members.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And by this time, sir, had you received any information concerning the advance or success of the VRS with respect to their attack on the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't hear anything in particular, nothing official at any rate, only what we heard, the rumours that had spread.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you hear, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at one point we heard that the army had taken Srebrenica and that there were some civilians in Potocari but nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as you advanced towards Potocari, sir, was your commander, Mr. Pantic, with the 1st Company as you proceeded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantic was with us all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about your platoon leader, Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you know how they were communicating with each other, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you know from whom Mr. Pantic was receiving his orders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how were orders communicated down the line, down the chain of command, during these couple of days, to yourself, for example? How was the information passed on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Raso must have transmitted it to platoon commanders and platoon commanders to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say "Raso", you're referring to Mr. Pantic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And before we move on, sir, what is your understanding as to the coordination, if any, between the army and the MUP when a unit such as your PJP unit is deployed into the area of responsibility of the army?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think our unit was superior to the troops -- sorry, resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'd like to have it clear in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I can ask a clarification question on that, Your Honour. I'll clean that up just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "resubordinated", can you just be a little bit more detailed about what you mean when you say "resubordinated"? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the army was the one that conducted combat activities and operations. We were just an attachment. We were engaged occasionally as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you began to enter Potocari, was your 1st Company alone or were there other police or army units that entered with you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one police detachment and there were some troops. I don't know which units.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say one police detachment, what are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the detachment of the Special Forces of the police, special units of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Special Police Brigade, sir? And this may be a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to troops, are you referring to just general VRS forces, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Members of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber, please, what path or route you took as you left from Zuti Most and entered Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we set out from the Yellow Bridge, Zuti Most, we took the left [as interpreted] side along the road to Srebrenica. After covering a certain section, there were no stragglers from the army, there were no civilians, there was no resistance, none at all, so at one point we descended from those hills to the main road to Srebrenica. Somewhere near the UN base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one, I believe that we need to make one correction for the transcript but maybe my colleague would do it. Here on page 46, line -- end of line 8 and beginning of line 9 he said we took the left side, and I believe that witness said something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What did you say, Witness? Did you say we took the left side or did you say something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thank you my learned friend for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just so that there is -- it's absolutely clear on the record, is that the right side with your -- as you're entering Potocari, sir, your right side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The right side looking from the main road going to Srebrenica and Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you encounter anyone as you were checking the houses and walking through that area before getting to the main road?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't find anyone, we didn't run into anyone, until we came close to the centre of Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you observe as you neared the centre, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when we got to that ribboned, cordoned off part of the road where there were UNPROFOR members or you mean earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir. Can you describe for the Court whether you encountered any civilians as were you coming down that main road before you reached the yellow tape or the cordoned off part of the road, as you described it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We came across a group of civilians who wanted to cross the road to go to the UN base. We told them not to be afraid, that they were free to pass through, and they did so without any problem, and they entered the UN base.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during this period of time, sir, as you're continuing further down that road, do you remember whether you were accompanied or in the presence of any particular soldiers whose names you can remember? And I will show you some photographs later in your testimony but do you remember the names of anybody at this point without seeing any photographs, of people that you were with, as you were walking through Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the army, I remember two of them. There were some more but I don't remember the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The two soldiers who you just referred to, do you recall their names?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one Milinkovic and the other one was Radenko Tomic. The first one was Mile Milinkovic or Milan Milinkovic, also known as Like.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you described reaching an area that was cordoned off. What did you see when you got there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to that ribbon, the cordon, there were some members of the army, members of the special unit of the police, as well as UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, sir, this may be a translation issue but when you say special unit of the police, are you referring to the Special Police Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how do you know that those individuals were from the Special Police Brigade, sir? Or how did you know that at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On their left sleeve they wore an insignia of the Special Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with respect to the members of the army, sir, did you have any knowledge as to which brigade they may have belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw later some soldiers that I knew were from the Bratunac Brigade. Others I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened after you reached this cordon?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got there to the cordon, we stayed there for a while, for a short while, until General Mladic arrived. When he arrived and got out of the car, he started yelling at us to get away from there. In fact, he was shouting at Mr. Ljubisa Borovcanin saying, "What do you need the police here for? We have the army. Get them out of here." So we left that area around the cordon. We went behind a house into an orchard. And that's where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw soldiers, Special Police Brigade members, UNPROFOR. Can you describe the civilians that you saw in this area, sir? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a large number of civilians, women, children, the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described going to a house, into an orchard. Do you know where that was located or can you describe where that orchard was located in relation to the UN base and any other features that may have been there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The closest reference point is a factory called Cinkara, the Zinc Factory. Looking from the perimeter of that factory, we were to the right in that orchard.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What happened next, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is nothing much to say. We just sat around there. I don't know for how long. We got something to eat. A bit later, I got in touch with some neighbours, two female neighbours from Srebrenica. Nothing special happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At some point, did you leave the orchard area, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one point I was with a number of other former neighbours who lived in Srebrenica close to me. I talked to them for a while, and then I returned to join the rest of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the same orchard where the rest of my colleagues were, and we stayed there until we left Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did you learn that it was time to leave Potocari? What was -- what were you told?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who exactly brought the message, but somebody said orders had come to leave Potocari and go to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you estimate at all how much time you spent in this orchard area by the Zinc Factory?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say precisely, maybe an hour, maybe two hours, maybe less. I don't know. I really can't say after all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During that period of time, sir, did you become aware that any vehicles were arriving to the base there at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the UN base?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's right, the area of the UN base.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Do you mean some vehicles were entering the base or do you mean the transportation vehicles for civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I understand why I asked a confusing question for you, sir. Did you see any vehicles arrive on that main road in front of the UN base?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my vantage point, it was impossible to see whether they were going into the base or not. I don't think anybody was going into the base. I think they made a U-turn there and parked, awaiting the boarding of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what kind of vehicles were those, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly buses, with some trucks among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how did you leave the area, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our bus came to pick us up. We all got into the bus and drove away to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in terms of these buses and trucks that you described, what were you able to see as you were leaving Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special. Vehicles coming, making a U-turn, setting themselves up to receive passengers. There was a crowd. Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see any soldiers or police deployed along the road near those buses, sir, as you were leaving?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At any time up to the time you left Potocari, did you see any Muslim men being separated from their families, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslim men detained?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not while we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslims boarding those buses that you saw on the road, parked on the road?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. Before we left, there were perhaps two or three vehicles parked there. At that time nobody was boarding the buses and nobody did until we departed. After that, I suppose some transports started.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did you go after leaving Potocari, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Potocari, we went to Bratunac and stopped by the department store in Bratunac, and stayed there for quite a while awaiting further orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we were waiting, time was long and some people drifted away. We talked about Zvornik, that it was threatened, that an attack was imminent, that we should go to Zvornik. I didn't receive any information from offices Pantic or Micic. At one point, when orders were given to board the bus again, we did so and we set off towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then what happened, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stopped at a place called Sandici. There were some army troops there and members of the Special Police Brigade who told us that they were occasionally being fired at from the nearby woods, and somebody then ordered, I suppose it was Pantic, that we get out of the bus and deploy along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not there were any other PJP units there as well when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just us.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where were you deployed, sir, along that road?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was deployed below the pass looking towards Sandici, and that's the area, the small area, that my unit covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What was your assignment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special. We were just told to stay there and secure the road, and probably, and we didn't even need to be told that, there were Serb villages behind our backs and we were supposed to guard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And guard them from whom or what, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Were you given any information or did you have any idea of where these Muslim units may have been from, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sandici, to the left, above us, hills stretch a long way, and shooting was coming from there. So we knew that Muslim units were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You described previously that you had information or there was talk about Zvornik being under threat of perhaps an imminent attack. Did you have any idea of what the source of that attack was going to be? What was that threat, from the information or rumours that you were hearing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Was there ever any discussion or information amongst yourselves about the Muslim men of the Srebrenica enclave and where they may or may not have been at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since we were already in Potocari, where there was no Muslim army, it was logical to assume they were around in the woods nearby and that they were trying to reach the territory controlled by the BH army. So we knew they were there somewhere. But precisely where exactly, we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: When you were deployed in this Sandici area, was Mr. Pantic, your commander, there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I was the last behind that pass. Most of them stayed near that destroyed house that provided cover. I was the last one behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any information as to whether your commander was in that general section of the communication that you were securing, although he may not have been in your immediate area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you deployed to your position, sir, did you see any heavy weaponry deployed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you describe those armoured vehicles, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one was a Praga vehicle and the other one was a BVP, a combat vehicle with a three-barrel gun mounted on it, and I think the next day a tank joined them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you know to which unit or to whom the tank and those other mechanised armoured vehicles belonged?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. My unit had none of those vehicles. So I assume they belonged either to the Special Police Brigade or to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you were in the field on previous PJP deployments, do you recall ever seeing the Special Police Brigade detachments or units using such equipment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you just briefly describe for the Trial Chamber, sir, what you did while you were deployed on that section of the road on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we arrived at Sandici in the early evening and we deployed there and we didn't move from those positions until the early morning. It may have been around 4.00 or 5.00 a.m., I don't know exactly. I was already asleep and most of my colleagues were asleep, when I heard this explosion and when the shooting started. I woke up and I opened fire myself, together with my colleagues. We moved to the other side of the road but there was a canal there, a ditch, dug for our protection and when the shooting died out, a truck arrived. I heard that some people had been wounded. I did not take part in their providing first aid and putting them on to this vehicle. I was ordered to go further up to a house that had been destroyed, to guard our right flank, to prevent the Muslim units from infiltrating into our -- or penetrating into our right flank.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of your colleagues who were injured?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think three police officers from Zvornik were wounded but I don't know their names. The colleague who was -- died, who died, was Zeljko Nikolic [as interpreted], a police officer from our station.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I note that the transcript indicates that the name of your colleague who died was Zeljko Nikolic. Is that the correct name, the correct --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions about the 12th of July, sir, before we move on to the next day. From the time you were first deployed in the Sandici area until those early morning hours of the next day, when you heard the explosions, did you see any Muslims surrendering or being captured in your immediate area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: While you were deployed along the road that day, did you see any Muslims at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just civilians who were being moved under UNPROFOR escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say under UNPROFOR escort, sir, what leads you to identify UNPROFOR as escorting?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there -- they had vehicles that were visibly marked and they wore uniforms that were unlike the uniforms worn by our forces, so that's how we knew they were United Nations troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we are on the early morning hours of 13 July, sir. You described moving to a destroyed house after the attack. What did you do from that point on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on my arrival to this house, there were two or three of my colleagues with me, I don't remember exactly. I found an old door and I lay down and went back to sleep. And then in the morning, I don't know when exactly it was, I woke up, maybe because of gunshot. I woke up and I looked out of the house. My colleagues were down on the road below that pass. They were having breakfast and I joined them. And I learned from them that this colleague of ours succumbed to his wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after we had breakfast, we stayed there waiting for our commander, Mr. Pantic, to approve our departure to Bratunac because we wanted to organise the funeral for our colleague, for our dead colleague, Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, see Mr. Pantic in person about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see him personally. I didn't speak to him. Our platoon commander did that, Micic, and when we were given the approval, we left Sandici.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: During that morning, sir, did you move your position at all along the road, in that time while you were waiting for Mr. Pantic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of the time I was there I spent down there where I was deployed, but at one point, just before we left, I was up there at this destroyed house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is that another destroyed house other than the one that you had spent part of that night in, the night of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a different house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Trial Chamber what, if anything, you observed occurring in that area of that other destroyed house?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, while I was down there below this pass, I saw a few persons coming down from the woods passing by that house, and they went up to a meadow and they were probably instructed to sit down there because that's what they did. They sat down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was this meadow on the same side of the road as this other destroyed house or was it on the other side?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was opposite the destroyed house.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time of day it was when you left the Sandici area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the morning, but I can't give you the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what did you do once you were in Bratunac, just generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we arrived in Bratunac, we went to see Zeljko Ninkovic's parents. We expressed our condolences and we discussed the organisation of the funeral. So we spent the entire day there, assisting to organise the funeral and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
